title: Arc Welding as it applies to Tractor Mechanic

lessons.title: Arc welding processes and equipment
lessons.html:
How arc welding works

Arc welding uses an electric arc between an electrode and the workpiece to create intense heat that melts the metal. The molten pool must be shielded from the air, otherwise oxygen and nitrogen make the weld porous and brittle. Tractor mechanics use arc welding to repair implements, brackets, drawbars, loader frames and cracked components.

Common processes

ProcessHow it worksTractor use
Shielded metal arc (SMAW, stick)Flux-coated electrode; flux makes shielding gas and slagField and farm repairs, thick sections, works outdoors in wind
Gas metal arc (MIG/MAG)Wire fed continuously with shielding gasWorkshop fabrication, faster and cleaner
Flux-cored arcTubular wire with flux inside, with or without gasOutdoor work, good penetration
Gas tungsten arc (TIG)Non-consumable tungsten electrode with argonAluminium and precise thin work

Machine and settings

Welding machines may be transformers, rectifiers or inverters. They supply AC or DC. DC gives a smoother arc and is preferred for most stick electrodes. Current (amperage) is set according to electrode diameter, plate thickness and position; use the electrode maker's recommended range. Too little current gives poor fusion and a sticking electrode; too much gives undercut, spatter and burn-through.

Electrodes

Electrodes are classified by standard codes that show tensile strength, positions and coating type. General-purpose rutile electrodes are easy to use on mild steel. Low-hydrogen electrodes are used for higher-strength steels and critical joints and must be kept dry, often in a heated electrode oven. Cast iron needs special nickel-based electrodes and careful technique.

Joints and positions

Common joints are butt, lap, tee and corner. Welding positions are flat, horizontal, vertical and overhead. Flat is easiest; vertical and overhead need lower current and good control. Thick butt joints are bevelled so the weld can penetrate fully.

lessons.title: Welding on tractors safely and correctly
lessons.html:
Protecting the tractor

Modern tractors are full of electronics. Welding current can travel through the frame and damage ECUs, sensors, alternators and displays. Before welding on a tractor:

  1. Disconnect the battery negative and, if the manual says, the positive and ECU connectors.
  2. Fit the earth clamp as close as possible to the weld, on clean metal, on the same part being welded.
  3. Never let welding current pass through bearings, gears, hydraulic cylinders or wheel hubs; the arc across these surfaces pits them.
  4. Protect hoses, wiring, glass and paint from spatter with fire blankets.
  5. Remove or shield fuel tanks and lines, batteries and hydraulic hoses nearby.

Preparing the job

Clean the area to bright metal by grinding off paint, rust, oil and galvanising. Identify the material: cast iron, mild steel and high-strength steels need different procedures. Drill a small hole at each end of a crack to stop it running, then grind a V along the crack before welding. Heavy sections may need preheating; check the manufacturer's repair instructions, especially for structural parts such as ROPS frames, which usually must not be welded or modified at all.

Technique

  • Strike the arc and hold a short, steady arc length.
  • Keep an even travel speed and electrode angle.
  • Remove slag between runs with a chipping hammer and wire brush.
  • Inspect visually for cracks, porosity, undercut and lack of fusion.

Hazards and controls

  • Arc radiation: ultraviolet light burns eyes and skin (arc eye). Use a helmet with the correct shade filter and cover all skin. Use screens to protect others.
  • Electric shock: keep gloves and clothing dry, check cables for damage, never weld standing in water.
  • Fumes: ventilate or use extraction; galvanised and painted metal give toxic fumes.
  • Fire: clear chaff, grass, oily rags and fuel; keep an extinguisher nearby; check the area after work.
  • Hot metal: mark hot parts and use pliers.

Follow the OHS Act 85 of 1993 and your workshop's hot-work rules.

Key points

  • Stick welding suits outdoor repairs; MIG is faster in the workshop.
  • Set current for electrode size, thickness and position.
  • Disconnect the battery and clamp the earth close to the weld.
  • Never weld or modify ROPS frames.
  • Protect eyes and skin from arc radiation and control fumes and fire.
